A Moser-spindle-free 5-chromatic unit distance graph on 2131 vertices in the plane

Jan Kristian Haugland Note: E-mail address: admin@neutreeko.net

1 Introduction

The Hadwiger-Nelson problem asks for the minimum number of colours χ\chi required to colour the points of the plane such that any two points at a unit distance apart receive different colours. It dates back to 1950, and for almost seven decades, the best bounds were 4≤χ≤74\leq\chi\leq 7 [7]. The lower bound comes from a 4-chromatic unit distance graph on 7 vertices, known as the Moser spindle; confer Fig. 1. The upper bound comes from a tesselation of the plane by regular hexagons with 7 colours such that the diameter of each hexagon is slightly less than 1, while the distance between distinct hexagons of the same colour is slightly greater than 1. In 2018, de Grey [2] found a 5-chromatic unit distance graph, thus proving that χ≥5\chi\geq 5. The first example had 20425 vertices, which was soon improved to 1581 vertices. During the following few years, smaller examples were found, especially by Heule [3, 4, 5], and the current record is 509 vertices by Parts [6].

All known small 5-chromatic unit distance graphs rely heavily on the Moser spindle, and a natural question is whether this is a structural necessity for non-4-colourability. Voronov et al. [8] answered this in the negative by constructing 5-chromatic unit distance graphs on 64513 vertices entirely free of the Moser spindle.

In Section 2 of this note, we present a 7-fold symmetric unit distance graph HH on 21 vertices. In Section 3, the arcs of HH are utilized to construct a graph G1G_{1} on 740 vertices for which (0,0)(0,0) and (0,3)(0,\sqrt{3}) have different colours in any 4-colouring. Combining four isometric copies of G1G_{1} yields a Moser-spindle-free 5-chromatic unit distance graph on 2131 vertices.

2 A unit distance graph based on the regular heptagon

For 0≤j<70\leq j<7, let

Pj=−γ2​(cos⁡(2​π​j7+π2),sin⁡(2​π​j7+π2)),P_{j}=-\frac{\gamma}{2}\left(\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{2\pi j}{7}+\frac{\pi}{2}\right),\,\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{2\pi j}{7}+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right),
Qj=α2​(cos⁡(2​π​j7+π6),sin⁡(2​π​j7+π6)),Q_{j}=\frac{\alpha}{2}\left(\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{2\pi j}{7}+\frac{\pi}{6}\right),\,\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{2\pi j}{7}+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right),
Rj=β2​(cos⁡(2​π​j7+5​π6),sin⁡(2​π​j7+5​π6)),R_{j}=\frac{\beta}{2}\left(\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{2\pi j}{7}+\frac{5\pi}{6}\right),\,\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{2\pi j}{7}+\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)\right),

and let HH be the unit distance graph induced by {Pj}0≤j<7∪{Qj}0≤j<7∪{Rj}0≤j<7\{P_{j}\}_{0\leq j<7}\cup\{Q_{j}\}_{0\leq j<7}\cup\{R_{j}\}_{0\leq j<7}.

Proposition 2.1.

The graph HH consists of a regular heptagon, two regular heptagrams and seven equilateral triangles, as shown in Fig. 2.

Proof.

By basic trigonometry, {Pj}0≤j<7\{P_{j}\}_{0\leq j<7} are the vertices of a regular heptagon, {Qj}0≤j<7\{Q_{j}\}_{0\leq j<7} are the vertices of a regular heptagram {7/2}\{7/2\} and {Rj}0≤j<7\{R_{j}\}_{0\leq j<7} are the vertices of a regular heptagram {7/3}\{7/3\}, all of unit side length, and it remains to verify that Pj​Qj​RjP_{j}Q_{j}R_{j} is an equilateral triangle of unit side length for each jj. To this end, we establish two identities involving α\alpha, β\beta and γ\gamma.

First, we have

tan⁡θ2=sin⁡θ1+cos⁡θ\operatorname{tan}\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta}{1+\operatorname{cos}\theta}

which yields

1sin⁡θ=1tan⁡θ2−1tan⁡θ\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}\frac{\theta}{2}}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}\theta}

and therefore

α+β+γ=1tan⁡π7−1tan⁡2​π7+1tan⁡2​π7−1tan⁡4​π7+1tan⁡4​π7−1tan⁡8​π7=0.\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}\frac{\pi}{7}}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}\frac{2\pi}{7}}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}\frac{2\pi}{7}}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}\frac{4\pi}{7}}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}\frac{4\pi}{7}}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}\frac{8\pi}{7}}=0. (1)

Second, we have in general

∑j=1n−11sin2⁡j​πn=n2−13\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}^{2}\frac{j\pi}{n}}=\frac{n^{2}-1}{3}

(for example, confer [1], identity (23)). Taking n=7n=7, it follows that

α2+β2+γ2=12​(1sin2⁡π7+1sin2⁡2​π7+…+1sin2⁡6​π7)=72−12⋅3=8.\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}^{2}\frac{\pi}{7}}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}^{2}\frac{2\pi}{7}}+\dotsc+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}^{2}\frac{6\pi}{7}}\right)=\frac{7^{2}-1}{2\cdot 3}=8. (2)

In view of (1) and (2), we have

{α2+α​β+β2=α2+β2+(α+β)22=α2+β2+(−γ)22=4α2+α​γ+γ2=α2+γ2+(α+γ)22=α2+γ2+(−β)22=4β2+β​γ+γ2=β2+γ2+(β+γ)22=β2+γ2+(−α)22=4\begin{cases}\alpha^{2}+\alpha\beta+\beta^{2}=\frac{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+(\alpha+\beta)^{2}}{2}=\frac{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+(-\gamma)^{2}}{2}=4\\ \alpha^{2}+\alpha\gamma+\gamma^{2}=\frac{\alpha^{2}+\gamma^{2}+(\alpha+\gamma)^{2}}{2}=\frac{\alpha^{2}+\gamma^{2}+(-\beta)^{2}}{2}=4\\ \beta^{2}+\beta\gamma+\gamma^{2}=\frac{\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}+(\beta+\gamma)^{2}}{2}=\frac{\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}+(-\alpha)^{2}}{2}=4\end{cases}

which is equivalent to

{(α2)2+(β2)2−α​β2​cos⁡2​π3=1(α2)2+(−γ2)2−α⁡(−γ)2​cos⁡π3=1(β2)2+(−γ2)2−β⁡(−γ)2​cos⁡π3=1.\begin{cases}\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{\alpha\beta}{2}\operatorname{cos}\frac{2\pi}{3}=1\\ \left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(-\frac{\gamma}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{\alpha(-\gamma)}{2}\operatorname{cos}\frac{\pi}{3}=1\\ \left(\frac{\beta}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(-\frac{\gamma}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{\beta(-\gamma)}{2}\operatorname{cos}\frac{\pi}{3}=1.\end{cases}

By the law of cosines, with (0,0)(0,0) as the vertex opposite either side of the triangle, each side length must indeed be equal to 1. ∎

To construct a 5-chromatic unit distance graph, we utilize the 84 unit vectors occurring as arcs in HH when viewed as a symmetric directed graph, sorted by their angles with the positive xx-axis. The edges of the regular heptagon and the regular heptagrams cover all angles that are integral multiples of π21\frac{\pi}{21}. If we multiply the vector Q0​P0→\overrightarrow{Q_{0}P_{0}} by 4​sin⁡2​π7=8​sin⁡π7​cos​π74\operatorname{sin}\frac{2\pi}{7}=8\operatorname{sin}\frac{\pi}{7}\operatorname{cos}\frac{\pi}{7}, we get (−3,4​cos⁡π7−1)(-\sqrt{3},4\operatorname{cos}\frac{\pi}{7}-1), so that the angle is φ=π−tan−1⁡4​cos⁡π7−13\varphi=\pi-\operatorname{tan}^{-1}\frac{4\operatorname{cos}\frac{\pi}{7}-1}{\sqrt{3}}, which lies between 14⋅π2114\cdot\frac{\pi}{21} and 15⋅π2115\cdot\frac{\pi}{21}. Accordingly, we put θ=21π​φ−14≈0.42363201413287\theta=\frac{21}{\pi}\,\varphi-14\approx 0.42363201413287 and define

u2​j=(cos⁡π​j21,sin⁡π​j21),u2​j+1=(cos⁡π⁡(j+θ)21,sin⁡π⁡(j+θ)21)u_{2j}=\left(\operatorname{cos}\frac{\pi j}{21},\,\operatorname{sin}\frac{\pi j}{21}\right),\,\,u_{2j+1}=\left(\operatorname{cos}\frac{\pi(j+\theta)}{21},\,\operatorname{sin}\frac{\pi(j+\theta)}{21}\right)

for 0≤j<420\leq j<42. The corresponding arcs in HH are listed in Table 1, where the indices of the vertices are taken modulo 7.

Lemma 2.2.

Suppose S={s1,…,sn}S=\{s_{1},\dotsc,s_{n}\} where 2≤n≤82\leq n\leq 8 and 0≤s<84​∀s∈S0\leq s<84\,\forall\,s\in S, and let (x,y)=∑s∈Sus(x,y)=\sum_{s\in S}u_{s}. Then we either have |x|>εn|x|>\varepsilon_{n}, or |y|>εn|y|>\varepsilon_{n}, or x=y=0x=y=0, where ε2=ε3=0.045\varepsilon_{2}=\varepsilon_{3}=0.045, ε4=ε5=0.0067\varepsilon_{4}=\varepsilon_{5}=0.0067, ε6=0.0016\varepsilon_{6}=0.0016, ε7=0.00089\varepsilon_{7}=0.00089 and ε8=0.00071\varepsilon_{8}=0.00071.

Proof.

It has been verified by an exhaustive computer search using standard double-precision floats that for each 2≤n≤82\leq n\leq 8, if |x|<εn|x|<\varepsilon_{n} and |y|<εn|y|<\varepsilon_{n}, then {us}s∈S\{u_{s}\}_{s\in S} form a combination of closed circuits, where each circuit lies in either HH or its image under an arc-preserving isometry. Thus, (x,y)=(0,0)(x,y)=(0,0). ∎

Remark.

An example of a closed circuit in HH is given by P3​P4​Q4​Q2​P2P_{3}P_{4}Q_{4}Q_{2}P_{2}, which implies that u0+u35+u22+u53+u72=0u_{0}+u_{35}+u_{22}+u_{53}+u_{72}=0. An arc-preserving rotation of HH corresponds to an even shift of the unit vector indices (modulo 84), while an arc-preserving reflection of HH corresponds to a fixed-point-free reflection of the indices.

3 Construction of a 5-chromatic graph

Definitions and notation: Following the terminology in [6], a monochromatic pair of vertices are two vertices that have the same colour in any kk-colouring for some given kk, and a non-monochromatic pair consists of two vertices that cannot have the same colour. A point AA in the plane and a sequence i1​i2​…​ini_{1}\,i_{2}\,\dotsc\,i_{n} of indices represent a polygonal path via the vertices A,A+ui1,A+ui1+ui2,…,A+ui1+…+uinA,\,A+u_{i_{1}},\,A+u_{i_{1}}+u_{i_{2}},\,\dotsc,\,A+u_{i_{1}}+\dotsc+u_{i_{n}}. The vertex set of a graph GG is denoted by V⁡(G)V(G). The mm-core of a graph is obtained by deleting vertices of degree <m<m repeatedly until only vertices of degree ≥m\geq m remain.

We start by constructing a graph in the plane for which A=(0,0)A=(0,0) and B=(0,3)B=(0,\sqrt{3}) form a non-monochromatic pair for k=4k=4. Intuitively, vertices that have a shorter total graph distance to AA and BB tend to be more significant for this purpose. Thus for n∈{5,6}n\in\{5,6\}, let TnT_{n} be the unit distance graph induced by all vertices on some polygonal path from AA to BB of graph length ≤n\leq n, such that each arc is in {uj}\{u_{j}\}.

By Lemma 2.2, since there is a path from BB back to AA using the vectors u56u_{56} and u70u_{70}, the endpoint of the polynomial path represented by AA and i1​…​ini_{1}\,\dotsc\,i_{n} with n≤6n\leq 6 is equal to BB provided ∑k≤nuik=(x,y)\sum_{k\leq n}u_{i_{k}}=(x,y) with |x|<ε8|x|<\varepsilon_{8} and |y−3|<ε8|y-\sqrt{3}|<\varepsilon_{8}. Hence, we can find the individual valid paths numerically.

Moreover, if (x,y),(x′,y′)(x,y),\,(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}) are two vertices of T6T_{6}, their mutual graph distance is at most 6, either via AA or via BB. It follows that they are identical if and only if |x−x′|<ε6|x-x^{\prime}|<\varepsilon_{6} and |y−y′|<ε6|y-y^{\prime}|<\varepsilon_{6}, and they can therefore be distinguished numerically.

Thus, it can be verified that |V⁡(T5)|=1042|V(T_{5})|=1042 and |V⁡(T6)|=12856|V(T_{6})|=12856. Unfortunately, (A,B)(A,B) is not a non-monochromatic pair in T5T_{5}, whereas T6T_{6} is rather large. However, we can maneuver between these two undesirable cases by defining a graph G0G_{0} induced by

V⁡(T5)∪{v∈T6\T5|v​ is adjacent to at least 7 vertices in ​T5}V(T_{5})\,\cup\,\{v\in T_{6}\backslash T_{5}\,|\,v\text{ is adjacent to at least 7 vertices in }T_{5}\}

and letting G1G_{1} be the 7-core of G0G_{0}. The latter graph consists of 740 vertices and 3985 edges. With AA and BB required to have the same colour, G1G_{1} can not be 4-coloured, as verified by the SAT-solver CaDiCaL, and it follows that (A,B)(A,B) is a non-monochromatic pair. Curiously, the unsatisfiable core retained variables corresponding to all vertices of this graph.

A set of polygonal paths from AA to BB covering all vertices of G1G_{1} is given in Appendix A.

Let V1V_{1}, V2V_{2} be isometric copies of V⁡(G1)V(G_{1}) obtained by rotating V⁡(G1)V(G_{1}) by an angle π3\frac{\pi}{3} clockwise around (−12,32)\left(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) and by an angle π3\frac{\pi}{3} counterclockwise around (12,32)\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right), respectively. I.e.,

V1={12​(x,y)​(1−331)+(−1,0)|(x,y)∈V⁡(G1)}V_{1}=\left\{\frac{1}{2}\,(x,\,y)\left(\begin{matrix}1&-\sqrt{3}\\ \sqrt{3}&1\end{matrix}\right)+(-1,0)\,\middle|\,(x,\,y)\in V(G_{1})\right\}

and

V2={12​(x,y)​(13−31)+(1,0)|(x,y)∈V⁡(G1)}.V_{2}=\left\{\frac{1}{2}\,(x,\,y)\left(\begin{matrix}1&\sqrt{3}\\ -\sqrt{3}&1\end{matrix}\right)+(1,0)\,\middle|\,(x,\,y)\in V(G_{1})\right\}.

The graph G2G_{2} induced by V1∪V2V_{1}\cup V_{2} consists of 1066 vertices and 6264 edges. Among the vertices (−1,0)(-1,0), (0,0)(0,0), (1,0)(1,0), (−12,32)\left(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) and (12,32)\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right), the only two that do not form a non-monochromatic pair are (−1,0)(-1,0) and (1,0)(1,0), which accordingly must form a monochromatic pair. Finally, consider the spindle G3G_{3} induced by

{(x,y),18(x+1,y)(715−157)+(−1,0)|(x,y)∈V(G2)},\left\{(x,\,y),\,\frac{1}{8}\,(x+1,\,y)\left(\begin{matrix}7&\sqrt{15}\\ -\sqrt{15}&7\end{matrix}\right)+(-1,0)\,\middle|\,(x,\,y)\in V(G_{2})\right\},

which is a graph on 2×1066−1=21312\times 1066-1=2131 vertices and 2×6264+2=125302\times 6264+2=12530 edges. It is not 4-colourable, since (1,0)(1,0) and (34,154)\left(\frac{3}{4},\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}\right) are adjacent, and each of them is in a monochromatic pair with (−1,0)(-1,0). On the other hand, a SAT-solver can quickly find a 5-colouring of G3G_{3}, thus establishing that it is 5-chromatic. It has also been verified that it does not contain the Moser spindle as a subgraph.
